final.title: Built for Marble: Poorly Pet brand film (9:16, 52.8s, 30fps)
final.concept: Follow the lead. One real photo opens and closes the film: Marble on a bluebell path, looking back at us, with her red lead running to our hand. Everything in between is her story repainted as living gouache memories, and the red lead carries it. It hangs unused on the hall hook, lies over her crate, sits coiled among the late-night research, is clipped back on in the 2025 garden, and finally runs from every dog to us. Poorly Pet is named by 1.6s and IVDD lands at 4.8s after one held breath. The three-note Marble motif only resolves when the paint washes away and the real dog returns: 'Built for Marble. Here for every dog.'
final.art_style: Premium hand-painted gouache illustration for a heritage British brand film, at the level of a contemporary editorial picture book or the background art of an award-winning animated short. Opaque matte gouache with visible dry-brush strokes on warm cold-press cotton paper, the paper tooth showing through. Painterly realism built from simplified, confident shapes with soft lost-and-found edges; no outlines, no ink linework, no flat vector shapes. Any animal is naturalistic and anatomically correct, with true breed proportions, exactly four legs, natural paws and real eyes with a small catchlight; never cartoonish, cute, chibi or caricatured. Cinematic, motivated natural light with soft bounce, gentle atmospheric haze and painterly depth of field. Restrained palette: deep teal-green shadows (#0A3A37, #0F4C48), sage and pale green midtones (#E4EED6, #F3F6F1), warm cream highlights, soft honey-amber lamplight and muted bluebell-violet accents, at low-to-medium saturation; a coral-red dog lead, wherever one appears, is the only saturated accent. Calm, tender, grown-up mood. No text, letters, numbers, logos, labels, watermarks, signatures or borders. No people, faces or hands. Not a photograph, not a 3D render, not glossy CGI, not anime, not clip art, not childish.

shots.beat: Hook: the real Marble looks into the lens. Her name is set on frame 0 and the brand is on screen by 1.6s.
shots.onscreen_text: This is *Marble*. / She's the reason / Poorly Pet exists.
shots.visual: The real photograph. Frame 0 is already a finished thumbnail, with no fade from black and no blur. We are close on Marble's face: her amber-brown eyes look up into the lens, her silver-dappled ears are soft, her tan eyebrow spots catch the dappled sun, and the pink harness and red lead show at the lower edge. 'This is Marble.' is already set on frame 0 in Domine 600, 92px, cream #F3F6F1, left-aligned at x 72, line box y 290-395, over a deep-teal top scrim. 'She's the reason / Poorly Pet exists.' (Domine 600, 62px, cream) sits beneath it at y 430-575. Her head stays below y 700 throughout, and the sunlit path behind her is soft.

PHOTO-CUT scale = PLATE scale x (1 + 0.02*sin(pi*t/6.4)) about the eye midpoint, so she lifts off the wood and re-registers exactly at 6.4s. shots.sound: A woodland field recording (a licensed UK spring wood: blackbird, wren, light breeze) is already playing at -30 dB on frame 0, so the film never starts from silence. If no licensed recording exists, omit it; never synthesise birdsong. Solo piano starts the Marble motif on frame 0: A4 at 0.0 over a rolled D2-A2-F#3 with sustain pedal, F#5 at 1.2, and E5 at 1.6, held and unresolved. shots.transition_out: Continuous camera move into S02 (same plate, no cut).

shots.beat: The diagnosis, with one held breath before IVDD lands: an early pattern interrupt for IVDD owners.
shots.onscreen_text: In 2024, aged three, / she was diagnosed with / *IVDD*.
shots.visual: The camera keeps pulling back until the whole of Marble stands on the path at registration frame R. Her body is angled away to the upper left, her head is turned back over her left shoulder, and the red lead runs from her harness down out of the bottom of the frame to our hand. Two lines in Domine 600, 62px, cream, sit at x 72, y 300-445. Then 'IVDD.' appears alone in Domine 700, 150px, cream, at x 72, y 465-610: the biggest word in the film. At R the top of her head sits at y 628, just below the type.
shots.layers: As S01: PLATE plus PHOTO-CUT, gobo, leak, night scrim, grain and vignette. A cool grade layer (#0A3A37, soft-light) waits at 0%.

shots.sound: The woodland air continues. At 3.20 the piano moves to Bm(add9) and answers in minor (F#4 at 3.2, D5 at 3.6, C#5 at 4.0), and the strings enter pp on B2/F#3. shots.beat: The real moment becomes a painted memory. Her eyes are the last thing to turn to paint, then we dive down the red lead.
shots.onscreen_text: HEADER (x 72, top edge y 240; enters 7.2 and persists through S05): 2024 · IT STARTED WITH MARBLE (the year rolls back 2026 > 2025 > 2024)
shots.visual: Three broad dry-brush strokes sweep the frame, and inside each one the photograph is replaced by its gouache twin, C01: the same Marble, path and lead, now in opaque paint on cold-press paper. A soft circle closes over her eyes last, so her real eyes look at us a beat longer than the rest of the world. The camera then dives down the painted red lead toward where it leaves the frame, until the screen is just the red line on painted earth. Only the header sits top-left; there is no other text, so the transformation has room to breathe.
shots.layers: BOTTOM: PLATE plus PHOTO-CUT at R. TOP: C01, aligned to the photo on three keypoints (the eye midpoint, the harness ring and the lead's exit at the bottom edge) with a 3-point affine, plus C01-CUT (Marble lifted from C01 with Background Remover), which follows the same parallax rule as PHOTO-CUT. The C01 group is revealed through the three C11 stroke masks (luminance, CSS mask-image) and then a soft circular mask. FINISH FOR ALL PAINTED SHOTS: a procedural paper tooth (feTurbulence, multiply 5%) that fades in with the strokes; the shared plate grade; 3% grain; a 16% teal vignette; and 4-6 slow pollen motes (soft discs 3-7px, 30% opacity) in the sunlit areas. The gobo continues.
shots.motion: 6.40-7.45, brush reveal: stroke 1 (bottom third) sweeps left to right 6.40-6.95; stroke 2 (middle) right to left 6.65-7.20; stroke 3 (top) left to right 6.90-7.45. Each mask translates from -110% to 0 with a -4° tilt (power3.inOut), and the stroke paths skirt her head. The photo and C01 share one transform (R x 1.00 to 1.04 about E), and the photo softens from 0 to 2px underneath so any misregistration reads as depth. 7.25-7.75, eyes last: a soft circle centred on E (radius 120px to 0, 12px feather) closes and her real eyes become paint. 7.20, header: the lime rule draws from 0 to 48px (0.4s). Anchoring the zoom on the bottom edge keeps the frame covered while the lead swings toward vertical. Render this move at 120fps and blend it for a real zoom blur in the last 0.5s. 9.20-9.60: match-dissolve into S04.
shots.sound: One harp cluster per stroke (6.40 D4-F#4-A4, 6.65 B4-D5-E5, 6.90 F#5-A5-B5), panned L, R, L with the strokes. At 7.50 a single soft harp harmonic, D6, as her eyes turn to paint. Harmony: Gmaj7 (6.4), Asus4 (8.0), A (8.8). The woodland air fades out 6.8-8.0 as we leave the real world. Under the dive the strings swell (CC11 40 to 85 over 8.2-9.4) with a low harp gliss falling 8.8-9.5. The motion is carried by the music, not a whoosh.
shots.transition_out: Match on the red lead (9.20-9.60): the painted lead, still travelling, cross-dissolves into the same red lead hanging still from the hallway hook in S04, about a third of the way in from the left.

As the camera pulls back we find Marble lying on the runner at the lower right, her back legs stretched out behind her, looking up at us. The frosted glass of the front door glows dusk blue, and warm lamplight spills from a doorway on the right. BESPOKE SCORE, 'Marble's Theme', written to picture. Render it with the existing engine (video/pro3/marble/score.py, FluidR3_GM via FluidSynth, 48 kHz); change BPM from 72 to 75. Tempo is 75 BPM in 4/4: one beat = 0.8s = 24 frames, one bar = 3.2s, and 16.5 bars = 52.8s. Every cut lands on a bar or half-bar: 3.2, 6.4, 9.6, 12.8, 17.6, 20.8, 24.0, 27.2, 30.4, 33.6, 36.8, 38.4, 40.0, 41.6, 44.8 (in-shot resolution) and 48.0. The home key is D major, and the illness chapters sit in the relative B minor. LEITMOTIF 'Marble' = A4-F#5-E5 (scale degrees 5-3-2). It stays unresolved on degree 2 for the whole film and lands on D5 (home) only at 44.8, as the real dog returns.

INSTRUMENTS (0-indexed GM programs): Acoustic Grand Piano (0); String Ensemble 1 (48), doubled by String Ensemble 2 (49) at -6 dB for width; Pizzicato Strings (45); Orchestral Harp (46); Celesta (8); Glockenspiel (9); Acoustic Guitar nylon (24); Pad 2 warm (89); Timpani (47); and soft cymbal swells (a ride cymbal rolled at low, rising velocities on the GM kit), used twice only. A reversed piano is made by rendering a piano chord stem and reversing it.

- Bar 1 (0.0-3.2, S01): Solo piano with pedal over a rolled D2-A2-F#3, with the pad holding D/A at -18 dB. The motif: A4 at 0.0, F#5 at 1.2, E5 at 1.6, held. Celesta F#6 at 0.8 (chime 1).

At 4.4 everything releases, leaving only the reverb tail: a 0.4s held breath. At 4.8 a low piano octave B1+B2 with F#2 (velocity 70, pedal), and cellos pp on B2 from 4.95, swelling to 6.4.
- Bar 3 (6.4-9.6, S03): Gmaj7 (6.4), Asus4 (8.0), A (8.8). Harp clusters, one per brush stroke: 6.40 D4-F#4-A4, 6.65 B4-D5-E5, 6.90 F#5-A5-B5. A harp harmonic D6 at 7.5 as the eyes become paint. A string swell (CC11 40 to 85) over 8.2-9.4 and a low harp gliss falling 8.8-9.5 carry the dive.
- Bar 4 (9.6-12.8, S04): Bm (9.6), G (11.2). The piano plays one chord per half bar with a minor fragment (F#5 at 10.4, D5 at 10.8, C#5 at 11.2). The cellos descend B2 to A2.
- Bar 5 (12.8-16.0, S05): Em7 (12.8), Em7/G (14.4). The strings drop out, leaving piano, pad and a sustained violin F#5 at pp. Tuned notes on the terms: piano B5 at 14.4 and F#5 at 15.2 (velocity 35).

A timpani roll on A2 starts at 40.8.

The motif pickups land on the paint wash: A4 at 42.4 (the eyes become real), F#5 at 43.2 (stroke 1) and E5 at 44.0 (stroke 3), on piano doubled by violins, with a harp figure on stroke 2 (43.6). SOUND DESIGN: organic, and almost entirely musical. (1) The one ambience is a real, licensed UK spring-wood field recording (blackbird, wren, light breeze) at -30 dB over 0.0-8.0 (fading out 6.8-8.0) and 41.0-52.8 (fading in 41.0-42.4 and out 51.0-52.8). Optionally the same recording's garden birdsong plays at -36 dB over 24.4-30.0. If nothing licensed is available, omit it; never synthesise birdsong. (2) Every other accent is a musical gesture from the sampled instruments: harp clusters on the brush strokes, string swells and harp glisses for the camera dives, reversed piano for the screen fly-through (24.0) and the window portal (33.6), and piano, pizzicato and timpani accents on the dog cuts. There are no noise-synthesised whooshes or brush sounds, no clicks, no key taps, no pops, no stock risers and no sound on type. There are exactly three tuned chimes (0.8, 28.4, 46.0) and two cymbal swells (23.2-24.0 and 43.2-44.8). Silence is used twice as an effect: the breath at 4.4-4.8 and the lamp going out at 17.3-17.6.

PRODUCTION AND MIX: Render each part as its own stem. Humanise velocity by ±6 and timing by ±8 ms, except the sync hits (0.0, 0.8, 4.8, 14.4, 15.2, 24.0, 28.4, 42.4, 43.2, 44.0, 44.8 and 46.0), which are exact. Write long CC11 swells on every sustained string note so chords never switch on and off in blocks, and layer the warm pad under the strings to hide FluidR3's thin attack. Use a convolution hall of about 2.4s with 20 ms pre-delay (piano 16% wet, strings 28%, harp 24%, celesta and glockenspiel 30%) and a 35 Hz high-pass on everything except the timpani. Cut the strings by 2.5 dB with a high shelf above 7 kHz and by 2 dB at 2.8 kHz to remove the nasal edge, and add 1.5 dB to the piano at 120 Hz for warmth. Pan the piano centre, the strings wide, the harp 20% left and the guitar 15% right, with the pizzicato alternating lightly left and right. Apply gentle 2:1 bus glue. The dynamic arc is quietest at 4.4-4.8 and 17.1-17.6 and peaks at 44.8, with the woodland bed sitting 12-16 dB under the music. Master limiter at -1.0 dBTP; integrated loudness -14 LUFS.

final.why_it_is_ad_ready:
HOOK AND BRAND RECALL (fixes the 'brand at 33s' weakness): frame 0 is the real dog's eyes, with 'This is Marble.' already set. It is a finished thumbnail, with no blur and no fade. 'She's the reason Poorly Pet exists.' is on screen by 1.6s, before the 3-second view mark. IVDD lands at 4.8s after a deliberate 0.4s musical breath, so Dachshund and IVDD owners recognise themselves early.

PACING (fixes the 'uniform middle'): beats change every 3.2-4.8s on the musical grid, and the pattern breaks every 6-8s. The breaks are: the held breath before IVDD; photo turning to paint with the eyes last; a dive down the lead; the lamp going out to black; a fly-through of the laptop screen into white morning; a 28-day calendar that fills and becomes a lit window; a portal into the window; a three-season eye-locked montage on half-bars; and the paint washing away so the real dog returns. Every transition is motivated by something in Marble's life (the lead, a lamp, a screen, the sun, a good day, a window, fairy lights, her eyes); none is a stock wipe.

ONE STORY, NOT AN EXPLAINER: the red lead runs through every chapter. It is taut to our hand, hung unused on the hook, draped on the crate, coiled among the research, clipped back on, hung on the chair, and finally running from every dog to us. One painter's world (13 gouache plates, one shared grade, one paper tooth) holds the graphic moments together. Lime stays a highlight, with no full-frame wipes. Story type is larger and calmer (62px, at most 3 lines of 24 characters).

CRAFT, NOT DOODLES: nothing is hand-drawn in code. Code only sets type, the marker band, the calendar dots, light and optics. Marble is painted into each plate with the photo and a C00 character sheet as references, and every cut-out is lifted from its own plate, so there are no pasted stickers. The risky crowd of breeds with people's legs is gone: three single dogs on Marble's own path, eye-locked, with no people.

IDENTITY ACCURACY: her coat was checked against the real photo. She is a chocolate dapple with heavy silver mottling on her head and ears, tan eyebrow spots and a liver-brown nose. Her pose was also checked: her body is angled away to the upper left and she looks back over her left shoulder. The registration points come from the actual 3574x2537 file: eye midpoint (1608,946), harness ring, and lead exit. Prompts and comp therefore line up with the photo that bookends the film.

SOUND (answers 'the sound effects are crap'): there are no synthesised SFX at all. The bespoke 75 BPM score uses real sampled instruments, and every cut lands on a bar or half-bar. Every accent is musical (harp, string swells, reversed piano, timpani). There are only three tuned chimes and two cymbal swells, plus a real licensed woodland bed or nothing. Silence is used twice. The 5-3-2 motif stays unresolved until the real Marble returns at 44.8, so the payoff is felt as well as read. The mix is -14 LUFS / -1 dBTP.

SOUND-OFF: every beat is told by on-screen copy taken from the Our Story page, one idea per screen, each held 2.0-5s.

CATEGORY AND CONVERSION: 'One place for guidance and carefully chosen products' appears at 34s, and the end card states 'For recovery, comfort and everyday wellbeing.' The end card carries the real dog in an arch, the typeset wordmark, POORLY10 in a print font, 4.6/5 from 99 reviews, free UK delivery over £39, the real-people promise and the URL, held fully composed for 2.2s.

COMPLIANCE: there is no mention of vets, AI, chatbots, scanners, quizzes or symptom tools. There are no bundles, urgency, brand counts or cure claims. The recovery line is the client's own wording, and all key text sits inside x 64-960, y 220-1480.

PRODUCTION RISK: 13 Canva generations plus 3 spares, within the 16 limit. The highest-risk image (C01 registration) has its own spare. Brush masks and the eyes-last circle hide misregistration, and the fast moves use bottom-anchored or point-anchored zooms, so plate edges never show.

CUT-DOWNS on bar lines with the music intact:
- 14.4s: S01 + S02 (0-6.4) + 44.8-48.0 + S14.
- 6.4s bumper: S01 + S14 build.

scores.strengths: Best single emotional through-line of the three: the red lead (taut in the real photo, hanging unused on the hallway hook, draped over the crate, coiled among the research, clipped back on in the garden). It says 'the walks stopped' without a word. Frame 0 is thumbnail-safe, with the real eyes and 'This is Marble.' already set, and IVDD is named by 3.4s, so Dachshund and IVDD owners recognise themselves early. Every transition has a motive (lead, lamp, sun, window, fairy lights, paint). The score is the most disciplined of the three: a 75 BPM bar grid and a 5-3-2 motif held unresolved until 'Built for Marble'. SFX are capped at six organic kinds and three tuned chimes, which answers the client's complaint about cheap sound. The C00 character sheet plus a shared comp grade is the most credible plan for consistency. The end card's arch window with the real photo looks premium.
scores.weaknesses: Weakest on brand recall. 'Poorly Pet' is not said or shown until about 33s, so the roughly 70% of viewers who drop off by 15s never learn whose ad it was. Category clarity is also weak: the only place it says what the brand is comes at 35s ('one place for guidance and carefully chosen products'), and the end card has no category line. Pacing is uniform (3.2-4.8s beats, every one a slow push or truck) with no mid-film pattern interrupt, so the middle third (S04-S07) is the most likely place for scroll-away. Story type at 56px with up to 4 lines of 27 characters is small for phone reading at feed speed. There is no product cue at all beyond an implied ramp and parcels.
scores.risks: Uses the whole 22-image budget. Marble is generated six times (C03, C05, C08, C11, C15 plus the C01 twin), and four of those are cut-outs composited onto separate plates (lying on a hallway rug, top-down asleep in a bed, standing in the garden, sitting on a chair). Each needs perspective, light and contact shadow to match, or it reads as pasted-on stickers, which is the 'cheap' look the client rejected. C16 is the highest-risk generation in all three treatments: five different breeds plus people's legs and boots in one image, where AI anatomy (extra legs, fused feet) is likely. The C01 painted twin has to register with the photo on three keypoints for the brush paint-over, and Canva image-to-image will drift; blur mitigates this but there is no retry slack. The plan relies on a licensed woodland field recording that may not exist.

scores.strengths: The strongest paid-social construction. It opens on the real eyes with 'Meet Marble. She's the reason Poorly Pet exists.', so the brand is on screen by 1.7s, before the 3-second view mark. It has the most deliberate retention architecture, with two pattern interrupts: a hard cut to silence and a 300px 'IVDD' at 11.25s, which is a thumb-stop for the core IVDD audience, and the 12x12 day-grid turning lime at 30s. The grid is the most ownable, shareable visual in all three treatments and makes 'better days outnumbered the bad' instantly legible with the sound off. The search chips ('dachshund dragging back legs', 'is she in pain?', 'best ramp for a dachshund') are high-relevance targeting copy; IVDD owners will feel seen. The empty lead and harness on the hook (no dog in frame) is quietly devastating. Category clarity is best: the rolling 'recovery. comfort. everyday wellbeing.' plus a 2.5s product glimpse without prices, the brace and ramp seen on Marble in S08, and an end card with proof, real-people service, offer and URL. Type at 64-80px is the most phone-legible. Sound is the most restrained: musical accents only, four near-inaudible whooshes, and silence used as an effect. Lowest image count (16), leaving about 6 retries.
scores.weaknesses: Mixed media can feel less cohesive. Painted plates, glass UI chips, a type-only IVDD card, a motion-graphic grid and two full-frame lime wipes risk reading as an explainer edit rather than one premium film. Lime used as a full-frame wash pushes the brand rule that lime is a highlight only. The six-dog pyramid on a flat pale-green field (S12) and the dog footer on the end card are the weakest visuals: painted cut-outs on a plain background drift toward pet-insurance stock or sticker lineups. Per-character typing with a blinking caret on the chips is the most 'template' motion in the film. S06 and S10 beat B are text-dense (a clock, a headline and six chips; a headline, a rolling word and three packshots in 2.75s). Transitions are mostly crossfades and wipes, plainer than the other two treatments.
scores.risks: Six separately generated dog cut-outs need one consistent painter's hand, and C11 as a style reference may not hold; this lineup is the most likely shot to look cheap. Marble is painted into several plates by text-to-image with the photo as a medium-strength reference (C05, C07, C09), so her coat markings may drift between scenes. QA every plate against the photo. Canva may render the back brace on a Dachshund wrongly; a fallback is specified. C01 has to overlay the photo for the brush reveal (mitigated by blur and three variations). The chips must read as the owners' own late-night searches, never as a Poorly Pet 'symptom search' feature, or they brush against the no-symptom-scanner rule. The harp plucks on each chip can turn twee if they are not kept well under the music.

scores.strengths: The most sophisticated filmmaking. A single eye anchor E holds the viewer's gaze across cuts, and 11 motivated transitions mean nothing ever just cuts. Standouts: the real eyes are the last thing to turn to paint; the light drains out of the same path for the diagnosis; the lamp click goes to darkness and then to laptop glow; the camera flies through the screen into whiteout and morning; the last lime 'good day' dot morphs into the lit Sandbach window; and a real photo print tucked in a kraft parcel zooms back into the real Marble, the best full-circle device of the three. The four-seasons 'every dog' montage (0.75s eye-locked cuts) shows 'Here for every dog' with energy right before the end card and stays in the painted world. The C20 clean plate (painted path with the dog removed) is a smart technical fix that makes the parallax free of artefacts. Brand is named by about 5s, and the end card has the clearest category line ('Carefully chosen for recovery, comfort and everyday wellbeing').
scores.weaknesses: Hook is weaker for the feed. Frame 0 is deliberately out of focus (rack focus lands at 0.8s) and the hook text starts arriving at 0.35s, so the thumbnail and first impression are soft. The end card is crowded (medallion, wordmark, two-line subline, three proof lines, offer chip and URL) with only a 1.8s static hold. No hard mid-film pattern interrupt; the interest comes from transitions rather than a stop-moment. The whip-tilt is the one move that could feel showy against the premium tone.
scores.risks: Uses 20 of 22 images, leaving only 2 retries, yet it has the most fragile image-to-image chain: C01 must register to the photo, C20 must remove the dog without shifting the composition, C02 is a relight of C20, and C15-C18 must put four different breeds' eyes on the same anchor in a Dachshund's look-back pose (a greyhound or Labrador in that pose is likely to warp). The 1400px whip-tilt will expose the plate edges unless the plates are generated taller than 9:16. The 20 celesta and glockenspiel notes on the dot fills (in about 2.4s) risk the 'twinkly sparkle' cheapness the client complained about, and sporadic laptop key taps are a literal foley choice. Marble is painted into plates several times by text-to-image with an identity reference (C06, C08, C10, C12), so coat consistency needs strict QA.

It shows 'every dog' inside the painted world and avoids the sticker or stock look.

From storybook: make the hook thumbnail-safe from frame 0. Have 'Meet Marble.' already set on frame 0 with the lime swipe completing by about 0.8s, rather than rising at 0.10s, and never open on a blurred frame.

From storybook: bookend with a real woodland field recording (birdsong and breeze under the real photo at the open and close; omit it rather than synthesise if none is licensed). From storybook and cinematic: tone down editorial's two full-frame lime wipes. Keep at most one, give it a dry-brush marker edge, or replace it with a motivated match (the grid's lime squares becoming sunlight already does this well), so lime stays a highlight rather than a wash.

scores.strengths: The most coherent piece and the most ready to produce. One physical motif, the red lead, runs through the whole film, and every transition has a story reason: the lead becomes the lead on the hook, the lamp bloom becomes the desk lamp, a dawn leak, the sun becomes a street lamp, the window portal, fairy-light bokeh becomes woodland dapple, and the painting repaints back to the photo. Frame 0 is a finished thumbnail: the real dog's eyes, with 'This is Marble.' already set and no fade from black. It has the best consistency system of the three: a C00 character sheet that never appears on screen, the photo plus C00 attached to every Marble image, C01 used as the style reference for every plate, and one shared grade so 20 generations read as one painter. It is the only treatment that dissolves the C16 world back into C01 behind a cut-out that is already pixel-identical. The bespoke 75 BPM score is the most musical design: the 5-3-2 motif stays unresolved until 'Built for Marble', the dynamic arc is mapped, and the mix notes are specific and fix FluidR3's thin attack (CC11 swells, pad layered under strings, EQ on the nasal edge). Sound design is restrained, with only three tuned chimes, which directly answers the 'cheap SFX' complaint. The end card is the cleanest and most premium: the real photo in a storybook arch, one proof line and a 2.4s composed hold. The copy is closest to the Our Story page, and it is fully compliant.
scores.weaknesses: The brand is late for an ad. 'Poorly Pet' first appears at about 32-33s, and the wordmark only at 48.9s, so anyone who drops off at 3-10s never sees the name. The rhythm is uniform. Almost every shot is a painted plate with a slow push, 3-4 lines rising top-left and one lime swipe, all on 3.2s or 4.8s bars. That looks premium but monotonous, with no pattern interrupt mid-film. 'Marble looks back over her shoulder' is used three or four times (S01-02, C11 in S08, S12, S13), so the garden beat feels repetitive. S12's procession of five breeds plus human legs is the weakest image idea, and the one most likely to read as AI. The S08-S09 day scrim switch to ink type breaks the dark-scrim system for only two shots.
scores.risks: The plan uses the whole budget (20 images plus 2 spares) with heavy reliance on cut-outs: Marble lying, asleep, standing and sitting, plus wellies, leaves, papers, tulips and bluebells, all pasted onto separately generated plates. Brushwork scale, perspective and light mismatches are the classic 'pasted sticker' tell. Canva Background Remover on painted fur can leave halos. C16 (a crowd of dogs and people from the knees down) has a high anatomy and cheapness risk. Canva may not accept two references at once (C00 plus the photo), so the core consistency method needs testing first. The S03→S04 lead match depends on C02 putting the hanging lead about a third in from the left; this is fixable by moving the plate. Registering C01 to the photo will never be exact; the blur and brush masks mitigate this. Brush textures and whooshes synthesised from pink and brown noise could sound like the cheap SFX the client rejected. The woodland field recording may not be available. The header at y 236 may sit just above the 220 safe line if 236 is the baseline. The breathing scaleY must stay sub-1% or it will read as puppetry.

scores.strengths: The most inventive editing grammar. An eye anchor E is locked across shots, and it hands off through eyes, lamp, laptop screen, morning doors, sunbeam, a single good-day dot, the lit window, a kraft box, a real photo print and back to the real photo. The film also ends with seasonal dogs locked to the same eye point and an iris that closes onto a medallion of the real Marble. The C20 clean plate (painted path with Marble removed) shows real comp know-how and gives parallax without artefacts. Her real eyes are the last thing to turn to paint, which is a beautiful, specific beat. Pushing into the photo print so its picture fills the screen is the best full-circle device in the round. The restrained 28-dot calendar on the sunlit rug, with the last good day morphing into the window, is a smart graphic metaphor. Shot variety (POV, overhead, exterior, flat-lay) gives it more film language than the other two. The brand line arrives at about 5.5s. The four-seasons montage at 0.75s per shot creates lift before the end card and hides generation flaws. The score is solid with a recalled bar 1, and the 'Real people' proof line is a good differentiator.
scores.weaknesses: Frame 0 is a blurred rack-focus with no text until 0.35s, which makes a weaker thumbnail than the storybook treatment. Eleven bespoke transitions risk feeling showy: the whip-tilt, the 4.4x fly-through into the laptop screen and the iris can tip into 'transition pack' if they are not perfect. The laptop at 2am and the screen fly-through are generic stock-ad imagery. The end card is dense: medallion, wordmark, a two-line subline, three proofs, an offer chip and the URL, about nine text lines inside 6s. Four dogs in 3s is very fast for some viewers. There is no character sheet, so Marble's consistency depends on C01 as the only identity reference. The coat brief contradicts the real dog: it describes 'mottled cocoa brown with chocolate patches', but Marble is a silver-grey dapple with dark patches and tan points.
scores.risks: The coat description could push every painted Marble brown, so she will not match the real photo that bookends the film. That breaks the central idea. Marble is painted into plates (sleeping by the table, walking up the ramp in full profile, curled overhead in a back support) without cut-out control. Short legs walking in profile is an anatomy risk. Seasonal dogs made image-to-image from C01: at high strength Canva may keep a dachshund, and at low strength the pose drifts, so eye-locking needs per-plate transforms that fight the 'one continuous camera' claim. The foley it asks for (lamp click, laptop key taps, tissue rustle, dry-bristle brush) has no source in the pipeline. Synthesised versions would be exactly the cheap SFX the client rejected, and the key taps are borderline anyway. It needs a 120fps render for the whip and fly-through, which is doable but slow. A 4.4x push into an upscaled raster relies on blur. It uses 20 of 22 images, leaving only 2 retries for a plan with many precise positional requirements (S at the screen centre, D, W, B).

scores.strengths: Has the strongest direct-response mechanics. 'Meet Marble. She's the reason Poorly Pet exists.' puts the brand on screen by 1.7s. A hard cut to silence and a 300px 'IVDD' type slam at 11-12s is a genuine mid-film pattern interrupt aimed at the highest-intent audience. The search-query copy ('dachshund dragging back legs', 'ivdd crate rest tips') is very relatable for IVDD owners. 'Light drains, then returns' is a clear emotional throughline. The 2026→2024 odometer rewind cleanly signals a flashback. The hallway shot with only the hanging lead and harness, and no dog, uses absence well. Most accents are musical, there are only four whooshes, and the deliberate silence is mature sound thinking. It uses the fewest generations (16), which leaves about 6 retries, the healthiest budget, and it is easy to build in the pipeline.
scores.weaknesses: It is the least cohesive and least premium. It keeps switching visual modes: photo, gouache, a type-only teal card, frosted-glass UI chips that type themselves with a caret, a 144-square day-grid that reads like a GitHub contribution chart or corporate infographic, a product shelf with packshots bobbing on sines, a sticker lineup of six dogs on flat pale green, and a pale end card. It reads like a motion-graphics template ad rather than a brand story. Two full-frame lime wipes push the highlight colour into a loud slide transition. Harp plucks on every chip turn the music into app UI sounds. The floating brace, harness and drops tip towards catalogue. The six-dog footer clutters the end card. 6% grain stepped at 15fps will look dirty next to the painted plates. There is no character sheet.
scores.risks: The six separately generated dog cut-outs composited on a flat background are the most likely to look cheap and 'clip-art pasted'. That is exactly what the client rejected, and it is repeated on the end card. Marble is painted into plates C05, C07, C08 and C09 using the photo at medium strength or text only, so her coat and face are likely to drift between shots. The C07 night to C08 day wipe needs Canva to reproduce the same table and bed position image-to-image, and any shift will show as a jump under the wipe. Rotating a rigid cut-out lead on a pivot looks fake if it is more than about 1°. The glass chips and typing look more like a tech or chatbot aesthetic than a warm British heritage brand, which is risky given the brand's no-chatbot positioning. pitches.title: Follow the Lead: Marble's Story (Poorly Pet brand film, 9:16, 52.8s)
pitches.concept: Follow the lead. In the one real photo of Marble, a red lead runs from her harness to an unseen hand. The film follows that lead into a painted storybook: it hangs unused on the hallway hook, lies over the crate, sits coiled among the late-night research, is clipped back on one spring morning, and then leads onto a bluebell path shared with every dog. At the end the paint washes away and the real Marble looks back at us. The real photograph opens and closes the film. Each painted chapter is joined to the next by a match on something from her life (the lead, a lamp, the sun, a window, fairy lights), and the score's three-note 'Marble' motif only resolves on 'Here for every dog'.

pitches.title: Better Days: Built for Marble (Poorly Pet brand film, 9:16, 54s)
pitches.concept: The film opens and closes on the real photo of Marble looking back at the camera. Everything between is her story repainted as living gouache memories, and the single idea that carries it is light. In 2024 the sun drains out of her woodland path. The late nights are lit only by a laptop. Then, as her better days start to outnumber the bad ones, the light comes back and the painting turns back into the real dog. It ends on the promise 'Built for Marble. Here for every dog.'

pitches.title: Built for Marble: Poorly Pet brand film (9:16, 54.0s, 30fps)
pitches.concept: The film is built on one real image: Marble looking back over her shoulder at us on a bluebell path. That photo becomes a painting, and each chapter of the story hands off to the next through a visual match. We go from her eyes to a lamp, a laptop screen, a morning doorway, a sunbeam, a single good day, a lit window, a packing box and a photo print, which brings us back to the real Marble. Her look back is then passed to every dog, across four seasons, and the film closes on her face.
